podcasts.title: HubSpot’s Co-Founder on Finding Your Next Startup Idea
podcasts.description:
As frontier AI labs expand into applications, where should startups build? a16z Partner Joe Schmidt joins HubSpot co-founder and CTO Dharmesh Shah to explore why the software opportunity is growing, and how founders can stay off the “Yellow Brick Road” the labs are racing down.

Drawing on HubSpot’s evolution, Dharmesh explains why founders should start with a narrow market, learn quickly, and solve the whole customer problem. They discuss where application companies can build lasting value as models become infrastructure: workflows, customer context, and the systems where work happens.

They also explore HubSpot’s AI experiments, the rise of one-person businesses, and why cheaper software creation could unlock markets that previously couldn’t support a software company.

podcasts.title: The biggest risk to the US data center buildout is already in effect in one state.
podcasts.description:
The biggest risk to the US data center buildout is already in effect in one state.

“The single biggest risk isn’t a single candidate, because in many cases both parties and candidates want developers to accept stricter terms.”

“In the case of Texas, it’s a freeze that already exists. Texas stopped issuing TCEQ permits to data center projects at the end of September, on top of an ERCOT interconnection audit that started in August.”

“Texas alone is close to 30% of US additions in 2028. So a few months of lost time in that one state, that one market, could move the national number.”

podcasts.title: Scott Kupor on Building a16z and Rebuilding the Federal Workforce
podcasts.description:
Scott Kupor helped build a16z from three people into a firm with hundreds of employees. Now, as Director of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, he’s applying some of the same lessons about talent, incentives, and organizational design to a workforce of roughly two million federal employees.

Scott joins Founders host David Senra to tell the story of a16z’s earliest days, from joining Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz during the 2008 financial crisis to borrowing Michael Ovitz’s CAA model to build a venture firm around specialized networks and services for founders. He explains why a16z chose to market itself when venture firms traditionally didn’t, how early wins like Skype accelerated the firm’s growth, and why it eventually reorganized around specialized investing teams.

Then they turn to Scott’s move into government. He lays out his effort to build a more merit-based federal workforce, attract younger technical talent, and create what he calls “permissioned risk” so government employees can actually try new things. That includes everything from changing how performance and promotions work to replacing a retirement process that still relied on hundreds of millions of pieces of paper stored in an underground Pennsylvania mine.

podcasts.title: The Health Interventions Actually Worth Your Time | Justin Mares
podcasts.description:
Health advice has become an endless stream of supplements, diets, wearables, and biohacks. Which interventions are actually worth your time? Truemed CEO Justin Mares argues that most people should ignore the extremes and focus on a few fundamentals: better food, movement, sleep, and reducing harmful exposures.

Justin joins a16z General Partner Daisy Wolf to walk through his own approach to health, from what he eats and how he exercises to supplements, blood tests, sauna, sleep, and the changes he’s made to his home.

They also discuss the larger problem behind Truemed: while chronic disease drives the vast majority of U.S. healthcare spending, relatively little goes toward prevention. Justin explains how Truemed is trying to change that by making it easier for eligible consumers to use tax-free HSA and FSA dollars on qualified lifestyle interventions.

podcasts.title: Jobs in the AI Era?
podcasts.description:
AI already writes better code than many of the engineers using it. Good engineers have never been more valuable. That may not last.

“Any software engineer that has their eyes on the ball will probably tell you that Opus, when given a well-specified problem, is just a better software engineer than me, period.”

“But at the same time, good software engineers are more valuable today than they’ve ever been.”

“Is it possible we’re in this Goldilocks zone, where humans can still provide the taste, supervision and judgment that makes them plus the model way, way more effective than just the model?”

“Maybe two years from now, you actually only need one dude at each company supervising all the software engineering, and basically everyone else got fired.”
